The rope in my hand is not mine. It is tied to my ankle, or maybe just my boot, but the knot is tight and the pull is steady. I do not look at the dark. I look at Mara. Her shoulder is still raised, braced against the weight of what she just saved, and her eyes are on the crate. The black water runs over the planks, soaking the goods we paid for in blood and breath.

I am breathing. I am alive. The beam is behind us, and the debt is in front of us, and the rope is pulling me toward the water that almost took me last winter. I do not fight the pull. I let it drag my heel across the wet stone, a slow, wet scrape. I want to tell her to cut it. I want to tell her to run. Instead, I let the tension speak for me.

"Mara," I say. My voice is rough, scraped raw by the cold. "The rope."

I do not ask what is on the other end. I do not ask why it is moving. I just point my chin at the line, tight and dark, and I wait for her to look at it, and at me, and choose.

The rope is not a suggestion. It is a claim.

I step over the broken planks of the crate, my boots finding purchase in the slick mud. The line tugs at Dell’s ankle, a steady, rhythmic pull that matches the pulse in the black water. I do not look at the dark. I look at the knot. It is a halyard knot, tight and final, tied by hands that knew exactly what they were doing.

I pull the knife from my belt. The steel is cold, and the edge is dull, but it will bite.

"Dell," I say. My voice is low, stripped of its usual ledger-keeping calm. "Hold still."

I kneel in the wet. The water rises around my knees, cold and thick. I wrap the line around my wrist, feeling the tension vibrate through the skin. I do not let go of Dell. I keep my hand on his shoulder, grounding him, keeping him from sliding into the dark.

Mara is watching me. Her eyes are on the rope, then on my knife, then on the crate that is already half-drowned. She is waiting for me to choose.

I cut the line.

The snap is sharp, a sound like a bone breaking. The rope goes slack, falling into the black water with a soft splash. The pull stops. Dell gasps, his breath shuddering against my hand.

I stand up. The knife is dripping. The debt is not gone; it has simply moved. It is no longer tied to his ankle. It is in the water, and it is coming for us.

"Mara," I say. "The cargo is gone. The debt is ours."

Mara’s boot hits the broken crate before the black water closes over it, and the whole thing bucks like a living thing. A second rope slaps the stone at Dell’s feet, tight and already moving, pulling toward the far end of the tunnel. Mara stands with one hand on the swaying crate and the other still holding Dell, the choice snapping back into her chest.

The crate slips from my grip, and the black water swallows it whole. I do not reach for it. I let it go, and I step back until my boots find the dry edge of the brick, where the air is still thick but not wet.

Kell is still holding the knife. The blade is dripping, a slow, steady rhythm that matches the drip from the ceiling. He is waiting for the facts. He is waiting for me to say that the debt was a mistake, or that the crate was worth more than the man, or that I hesitated.

I do not hesitate.

"I chose him," I say. My voice is steady, though my hands are still shaking where I hold them at my sides. "I chose Dell. I chose the man over the wood, and I chose the debt over the cargo. That is the fact."

I look at Kell. I do not look at the dark. I do not look at the place where the crate used to be.

"If I had taken the crate, the debt would have been his," I continue. "It would have been tied to his ankle, and he would have drowned in the water that was already rising. I took the weight. I took the cold. I took the choice. That is what a cargo master does. We do not weigh the wood against the blood. We weigh the blood against the debt, and we pay the debt."

Kell does not move. The knife is still in his hand. The water is still rising.

"The cargo is gone," I say. "The debt is ours. That is the fact."

I turn to Dell. He is still standing in the shallows, his face pale, his eyes fixed on the dark. I do not ask if he is okay. I do not ask if he is cold. I just look at him, and I wait for him to see me.

"I made the choice," I say to him. "I made it for us. And I will not make it again."

The tunnel breathes around us, cold and damp. The water laps at the brick, a slow, wet heartbeat. I stand where the light ends, and I hold my ground.

Mara’s voice snaps the tunnel’s silence open, and the crate slides from her hands into the black water. Kell’s knife dips an inch toward the current, and the rising flood answers with a slow, hungry lapping against the brick.

Dell’s boot scrubs the slick brick as the water surges around him, and the current seizes the edge of his coat. From the dark far end of the tunnel, a chain shudders up through the black water, dragging a wet shape toward the light.

The chain does not pull. It drags.

I feel the vibration in the stone before I hear it, a low, grinding shudder that climbs up through my boots and settles in my teeth. The water surges, no longer a slow lap but a rush, and it takes my coat. The fabric tightens against my ribs, cold and heavy, and I do not fight it. I let it pull me toward the center of the tunnel, away from the brick, away from the light.

Mara is still standing on the dry edge. Kell is still holding the knife. They are both looking at the dark.

I look at the shape moving through the black water. It is not a rope. It is a body, or a bag, or a debt made wet. It drags itself toward us with a slow, wet patience that I know in my bones. I do not reach for the chain. I do not reach for the knife. I just stand there, breathing in the damp air, and wait for the silence to break.

I say nothing.

The silence is not empty. It is heavy. It presses against my ribs, against the knot in my chest that has been there since the beam fell. I wait for the sound of the water to change. I wait for the pull to return. I wait for one of them to say something that will make it real.

I say nothing.

The wet shape breaks the black water ahead of Dell, and its chain whips around his boot before he can step back. Kell’s knife jumps toward Mara’s throat, and the tunnel’s drip stops as if the dark has heard her defense.

The chain is tight.

I do not look at the wet shape. I look at the knot in the steel, at the place where the metal bends around the leather of Dell’s boot. I pull the knife back. The edge catches the light, then the dark takes it.

Mara’s hand is on my wrist. Her fingers are cold, and they do not shake. I let them hold me. I do not push her away. The ledger is not a shield. It is a record.

I look at Dell. He is not looking at me. He is looking at the shape, and the shape is not moving. It is waiting.

I step over the chain. The water rises to my knee, and I do not stop. I walk to the brick wall, where the light ends, and I press my back against the stone. The cold is a fact. The water is a fact. The debt is a fact.

I take out the book. The pages are wet, but the ink is dry. I write the date. I write the name. I write the cost.

"Dell," I say. My voice is low, stripped of its usual calm. "Mara chose you."

I do not look up from the page. I write the word again, slower this time, pressing the nib into the wet paper until it tears.

"The cargo is gone. The debt is ours. And now, the water is paying."

The chain tightens around Dell’s boot and drags him sideways toward the dark, the wet shape’s head breaking the surface just below his ribs. Mara steps into the knee-deep water and shoves her shoulder against the shape, forcing it back from Dell. Kell’s torn ledger page slides off the brick into the current, and the ink bleeds across the black surface.

The shape is not a thing. It is a bill.

I do not let go of it. My shoulder stays pressed into the wet mass, and I feel the cold seep through my coat, but I do not step back. I do not look at the knife. I look at Kell.

"The cargo was wood," I say. My voice is steady, though the water is still rising around my knees. "The debt was not. If I had held the crate, we would have had a ledger and a body. If I held Dell, we have a ledger and a man. The wood rots. The man remembers."

I shift my weight, forcing the shape back an inch. The chain pulls at Dell, and I feel the tension in the line, tight as a bowstring.

"You want the facts," I tell him. "Here is the fact. I chose the one who could pay the debt with his life, not the one who could only pay with his value. The value is gone. The life is here. That is not a mistake. That is the price."

I hold my ground. The water is black, and it is cold, and it is mine.

I am here, in the wet, and the water is rising around my knees.

I look at him. His eyes are wet, and his face is tight with the weight of what he has just seen. He is not holding the knife. He is holding his breath.

"Write it down," I say. "The cargo is gone. The debt is ours. And Dell is here."

I do not move. I do not look at the dark. I stand in the water, and I wait for him to write the fact.

The chain goes slack, and the weight behind me vanishes.

I come up.

The black water breaks over my face, cold and sharp, and I gasp. The sound is too loud, too ragged, a tearing noise that fills the tunnel. I do not blink. I do not wipe my eyes. I just hang there, suspended in the current, my lungs burning with the effort of breathing again.

She is still standing in the deep, her shoulder pressed into the wet mass. Her face is pale, and her eyes are fixed on me. She is waiting for me to write the fact. She is waiting for me to balance the books.
